docs.title: Lab 4 — Operating system installation and identity
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This creates the Windows and Linux endpoints used by the SIEM and SOC labs. Use x64 media on the Windows PC and ARM64 media on the Apple-silicon Mac.

docs.title: A. Windows Server on the Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Download the current Windows Server Evaluation ISO from Microsoft's Evaluation Center. Check the release's evaluation period and terms.
  2. Create a Generation 2 Hyper-V VM (or supported VMware VM): name PSV-DC01; 2–4 vCPU; 6 GB RAM; 80 GB disk; NIC on SERVER segment; UEFI and supported Secure Boot template.
  3. Install Desktop Experience for GUI learning, patch the OS and install guest integration tools.
  4. Set a static address such as 10.10.30.10/24. Configure a gateway only if the lab router exists.
  5. Rename and reboot:
Rename-Computer -NewName "PSV-DC01" -Restart
  1. Install AD DS and DNS, then create the private lab forest:
Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services,DNS -IncludeManagementTools
Install-ADDSForest -DomainName "lab.psv.test" -DomainNetbiosName "PSVLAB" -InstallDNS

Follow the prompts and set a unique Directory Services Restore Mode password. The server reboots after promotion. Use the reserved .test namespace, not a domain you do not own.

  1. Verify:
Get-ADDomain
Get-ADForest
Get-Service NTDS,DNS
dcdiag /v
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.psv.test
  1. Create synthetic lab OUs/users only. Do not use real employee identities. Keep domain-controller DNS pointed to itself; configure DNS forwarders only if update access is required.

docs.title: B. Windows 11 endpoint on the Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Download official Windows 11 x64 media.
  2. Create VM: 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk, Generation 2, virtual TPM and Secure Boot as required by Windows 11/hypervisor, NIC on ENDPOINT.
  3. Install a Windows edition that supports the domain-join features you intend to practise. Patch and install guest tools.
  4. Set DNS to 10.10.30.10. Verify the domain controller resolves.
  5. Join the lab domain:
Add-Computer -DomainName "lab.psv.test" -Credential (Get-Credential) -Restart

Use a delegated join account rather than Domain Admin for routine joining. Verify after reboot:

systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"Domain"
nltest /dsgetdc:lab.psv.test

If joining fails, investigate DNS, time skew, routing, firewall policy and join permissions; do not disable security controls as a shortcut.

docs.title: C. Apply Windows audit policy with Group Policy
docs.text:
After the Windows endpoint is joined to the lab domain, use Group Policy Management on PSV-DC01:

  1. Create a GPO named PSV-Lab-Endpoint-Auditing and link it to the Lab-Workstations OU.
  2. Under Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → System Audit Policies, enable:
  3. Account Management → Audit Security Group Management: Success.
  4. Detailed Tracking → Audit Process Creation: Success.
  5. Logon/Logoff → Audit Logon: Success and Failure for this lab OU.
  6. Under Administrative Templates → System → Audit Process Creation, enable Include command line in process creation events if you need Event 4688 command-line evidence. Command lines can contain secrets; keep this lab-only and sanitise evidence.
  7. If practising PowerShell logging, enable Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows PowerShell → Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging on the lab OU only. Script contents can contain sensitive data.
  8. On the endpoint run gpupdate /force, then gpresult /h C:\\Temp\\gpresult.html. Confirm the policy applied.
  9. Make a controlled local group membership change on the disposable endpoint. Confirm Event ID 4732 and TargetSid S-1-5-32-544 for the built-in local Administrators group. The event proves a group membership change occurred; it does not prove malicious intent.

Do not apply this test GPO to production systems. Audit policy changes should be approved, event volume measured, and the GPO unlinked/removed after the lab if no longer required.

docs.title: C. Ubuntu Server on either host
docs.text:
Download the matching architecture ISO from Ubuntu and verify its published SHA-256 checksum. Create a VM with 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 40–60 GB disk, and the appropriate SERVER or ENDPOINT NIC. Install a named non-root user; enable OpenSSH only if needed.

sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
lsblk -f
ip -br address
ip route
systemctl --failed

Expected architecture: x86_64 on Windows PC; aarch64 on Apple Silicon Mac.

Optional audit telemetry:

sudo apt install -y auditd audispd-plugins
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd
sudo auditctl -s

Add only the audit rules needed for the exercise and measure event volume before forwarding.

docs.title: D. Kali Linux
docs.text:
Download the official Kali image matching the host/guest architecture and verify the checksum. Create a VM with 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM and 60 GB disk. Attach it only to REDTEAM; use temporary NAT only for updates and disconnect it before testing.

sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
ip -br address
ip route

Use Kali repositories for tools. Start with Nmap, Wireshark, Burp Suite Community and browser developer tools. Test only lab-owned targets.

docs.title: E. Windows 11 ARM on the Mac
docs.text:
Use Microsoft's official Windows 11 ARM ISO and a virtualisation application that explicitly supports Windows 11 ARM. Configure the required virtual TPM and Secure Boot using the hypervisor wizard. Start with 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM and 80 GB disk. Install, activate with a valid licence, update, and verify System type reports ARM-based processor.

Do not install x64 Windows media in an ARM VM. Confirm that every endpoint agent, driver and security product supports Windows ARM before relying on it.

docs.title: F. Baseline evidence
docs.text: For each VM record ISO URL/checksum, OS build, architecture, hypervisor/version, CPU/RAM/disk, virtual NIC and IP. Patch the VM, create a clean snapshot, and verify it restores. A snapshot is not a backup, especially for domain controllers or SIEM databases.

docs.title: Lab 9 — Isolated penetration-testing environment
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This is a controlled assessment lab. Only scan or test the targets you own and have deliberately placed in the isolated lab segment. Do not use the lab network as a bridge to your home, employer or public networks.

docs.title: 1. Topology
docs.text:
• Kali Linux: REDTEAM network, no bridged adapter.
  • OWASP Juice Shop: DMZ network, no direct home LAN access.
  • Optional Ubuntu target: DMZ network, patched base OS with a deliberately vulnerable application only.
  • Admin workstation: MGMT only.
  • Firewall/router: explicit allow from Kali to target IP and ports only.

Use the Windows PC for x86-64 targets or Mac for ARM64 Kali and container images with a matching platform manifest. Verify Docker images support the guest architecture before pulling.

docs.title: 2. Install OWASP Juice Shop with Docker
docs.text:
Use a supported Docker Engine installation on a disposable Ubuntu target VM connected only to DMZ. Follow Docker's official install guide for that Ubuntu release.

After installing Docker, verify:

docker version
docker info

Run the official OWASP Juice Shop image on the DMZ interface only. First inspect image metadata and confirm platform support. Bind the application port to the target VM's DMZ address, not to all host interfaces:

docker pull bkimminich/juice-shop
docker run -d --name juice-shop --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 10.10.60.20:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop
docker ps

Replace 10.10.60.20 with the actual DMZ address assigned to the target VM. If the image does not publish a compatible ARM64 manifest, use a supported x86-64 target on the Windows PC rather than assuming emulation is suitable.

From Kali, confirm only the intended application port is reachable:

curl -I http://10.10.60.20:3000

Do not expose this service on the home LAN or public Internet. Do not use default port mapping without binding to the lab interface.

docs.title: 3. Establish a test scope
docs.text:
Create a written scope file with: - Authorised tester VM/IP. - Target VM/IP and application URL. - Permitted ports and protocols. - Test window. - Excluded systems and networks. - Stop conditions. - Data handling and cleanup.

Example scope: Kali 10.10.40.10 may assess Juice Shop 10.10.60.20 TCP/3000 only. No other addresses or ports are in scope.

docs.title: 4. Reconnaissance and service identification
docs.text:
From Kali, first confirm the target address and then scan only the target and port in scope:

nmap -sT -sV -p 3000 10.10.60.20

Record the command, Nmap version, time, target and output. Do not use broad subnet scans until the lab's authorised scope explicitly permits them.

docs.title: 5. Web assessment workflow
docs.text:
Use browser developer tools and Burp Suite Community: 1. Configure the browser to proxy through Burp's local listener. 2. Confirm only the browser traffic for the Juice Shop lab is proxied. 3. Browse the application and map routes, requests, authentication state and API endpoints. 4. Test input validation, authentication and session handling, access control, business logic and error handling using the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide as the methodology. 5. Use harmless test data and avoid destructive actions. 6. Capture request/response evidence with secrets and personal data redacted. 7. Record finding, impact, reproducible steps, evidence, remediation and retest result.

Do not run destructive exploit chains, denial-of-service tests or tests against public sites as part of this lab.

docs.title: 6. Vulnerability verification and remediation
docs.text:
For each finding: - Reproduce in the isolated target. - Identify the affected component and version. - Check the vendor advisory and relevant OWASP guidance. - Explain preconditions and impact. - Propose a fix. - Apply the fix or configuration change in a separate snapshot. - Repeat the exact test and record whether it is resolved.

A scanner finding is not confirmed until manually validated. Avoid presenting tool output alone as proof of exploitability.

docs.title: 7. Cleanup
docs.text:
Stop and remove the disposable target when finished:

docker stop juice-shop
docker rm juice-shop

Revert the target VM snapshot. Remove temporary firewall allows and verify that the target is no longer reachable from Kali or any other network.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Apple-silicon MacBook host and hypervisor setup
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This guide is for M-series Apple-silicon Macs. VMware Fusion on Apple Silicon runs 64-bit ARM guests only; x86-64 operating-system images do not run as Fusion guests. UEFI firmware is required. Use the Broadcom Compatibility Guide to confirm support for the exact guest OS release.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
Open Terminal:

uname -m
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
sw_vers
df -h /
sysctl hw.memsize

Expected host architecture: arm64. Record chip, unified memory, macOS version and free SSD capacity.

  1. Update macOS through System Settings after backing up important data.
  2. Ensure sufficient free space; use a fast SSD for VM storage.
  3. Do not disable macOS security protections simply to make a VM install.
  4. Create ~/CyberLab/{ISO,VMs,Evidence,Exports} or an equivalent external SSD directory.

docs.title: 2. Install VMware Fusion
docs.text:
1. Download VMware Fusion from Broadcom's official desktop hypervisor portal.
  2. Confirm the package supports the installed macOS version and Apple-silicon host.
  3. Install, launch and approve only the system permissions requested by the installer.
  4. Review the current licensing terms during setup.
  5. Create a small ARM Linux VM as a smoke test.
  6. For ARM guests, use UEFI firmware, virtual NVMe storage and vmxnet3 networking where the guest/hypervisor wizard offers those settings.

docs.title: 3. Install Kali ARM64
docs.text:
1. Download the official Kali Apple Silicon/ARM64 installer or VMware image.
  2. Verify SHA-256 against the checksum published alongside the image:
shasum -a 256 ~/CyberLab/ISO/<downloaded-file>
  1. Compare the output exactly with the official checksum. Stop if it differs.
  2. In Fusion, create a VM from the ARM64 ISO/image.
  3. Suggested starting allocation: 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 60–80 GB disk, one NIC on the isolated assessment network.
  4. Complete the install, update Kali, and install open-vm-tools only if recommended for that guest image.
  5. Verify:
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
ip -br address
ip route

Expected architecture: aarch64 or arm64, depending on the command.

docs.title: 4. Install Ubuntu Server ARM64
docs.text:
1. Download Ubuntu Server ARM64 media from Ubuntu's official page.
  2. Verify its published checksum.
  3. Create a Fusion VM from the ARM64 image: 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 40–60 GB disk.
  4. Install a non-root user; enable OpenSSH only if remote administration is required.
  5. Update and verify:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
uname -m
lsb_release -a
ip -br address

docs.title: 5. Windows 11 ARM guest
docs.text:
1. Download Windows 11 ARM media from Microsoft's official page.
  2. Create a Windows 11 ARM VM using Fusion's supported wizard.
  3. Configure virtual TPM and Secure Boot as required by the wizard.
  4. Allocate 4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM and 80 GB disk as a starting point.
  5. Install Windows, activate using a valid licence, update, and confirm System type reports an ARM-based processor.

Important limitations: VMware documents limited VMware Tools functionality for Windows ARM guests. Nested-virtualisation-dependent features including VBS, WSL2, Windows Sandbox and Windows Defender Application Guard do not function in this configuration. Do not plan to run Docker Desktop with its WSL2 backend inside this guest. Use a separate Ubuntu ARM VM for Docker-based vulnerable applications. Check endpoint-agent and EDR vendor support for Windows ARM before using this guest to represent a managed enterprise endpoint.

docs.title: 6. Configure virtual networking
docs.text:
Identify Fusion's shared/NAT and host-only networks. Use NAT only for temporary OS updates and host-only/private networking for lab traffic. Do not connect Kali or intentionally vulnerable targets to bridged networking.

Fusion host-only networks and Windows Hyper-V private switches are local to each host. They are not automatically Layer-2 connected. Cross-host connectivity needs a deliberate lab firewall/router or separate isolated labs forwarding telemetry over a controlled management network.

docs.title: 7. Snapshot and verify
docs.text:
1. Shut down each VM cleanly.
  2. Create a baseline snapshot.
  3. Restore one snapshot to test recovery.
  4. Confirm guest architecture and NIC segment.
  5. Verify Kali/target cannot reach the home LAN.
  6. Record Fusion version, macOS build, ISO checksum, VM settings and network plan.

docs.text:

docs.title: Lab 1 — Windows PC host and hypervisor setup
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This page prepares a Windows x64 PC as the primary host for Windows/Linux guests, Splunk Enterprise, Elastic, Wazuh and Security Onion. Choose one primary hypervisor for the first build. Do not install several hypervisors and change Windows hypervisor settings repeatedly without a reason.

docs.title: 1. Preflight
docs.text:
1. Confirm Windows edition and build using winver.
  2. Confirm x64 architecture, RAM, CPU model and free disk using Hardware and platform compatibility.
  3. Back up important host data.
  4. Update Windows and firmware through the PC manufacturer's supported process.
  5. Enter UEFI/BIOS and enable Intel VT-x/VT-d or AMD-V/IOMMU if available. Save and reboot.
  6. Keep BitLocker recovery key accessible before firmware changes.
  7. Create a dedicated VM folder on a fast SSD, for example D:\VMs. Do not place active VMs in OneDrive-synchronised folders.

Verify virtualisation:

systeminfo.exe
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object HypervisorPresent, TotalPhysicalMemory

If Windows reports a hypervisor already present, that does not by itself indicate a fault; Hyper-V, Virtual Machine Platform, WSL2 and Virtualisation-Based Security can use the Windows hypervisor.

docs.title: Option A — Hyper-V
docs.text:
Use this if your Windows edition exposes the Hyper-V feature and the hardware prerequisites are met.

  1. Open Settings → System → About and confirm Windows edition.
  2. Open Turn Windows features on or off.
  3. Enable Hyper-V, including Management Tools and Platform, if available.
  4. Reboot.
  5. Open Hyper-V Manager and confirm the local host appears.
  6. In Hyper-V Manager, open Virtual Switch Manager. Create:
  7. an Internal switch for host-to-VM management traffic;
  8. one or more Private switches for VM-only lab segments.
  9. Do not use an External switch for Kali or vulnerable targets. An External switch bridges to a physical network and can expose the lab to the home LAN.
  10. Record switch names and purpose.

PowerShell verification:

Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V-All
Get-VMSwitch | Format-Table Name, SwitchType, NetAdapterInterfaceDescription

Hyper-V switch types: - Private: VM-to-VM only; host cannot communicate through that switch. - Internal: VM-to-VM and host-to-VM; no direct physical LAN connection. - External: connected to a physical network adapter; use only where explicitly required and understood.

docs.title: Option B — VMware Workstation Pro
docs.text:
Use this where Hyper-V is unavailable or you prefer VMware's VM networking workflow.

  1. Download VMware Workstation from the official Broadcom/VMware desktop hypervisor portal.
  2. Verify the installer source and publisher signature.
  3. Run the installer as an administrator and accept the licence terms shown.
  4. Reboot if requested.
  5. Open VMware Workstation and create a disposable test VM to verify the hypervisor works.
  6. Open Edit → Virtual Network Editor (elevate if requested).
  7. Identify:
  8. VMnet8 NAT network for controlled package updates;
  9. VMnet1 host-only network for host-to-VM management;
  10. additional host-only/custom networks for isolated lab segments.
  11. Disable host connection on a segment if it should be VM-only, and do not bridge the attacker/target segment to the physical adapter.
  12. Record subnet, DHCP range, host adapter and NAT status for each VMnet.

VMware menu names and licensing screens may vary by release. Follow the current product documentation for the exact version installed.

docs.title: 3. Storage layout
docs.text:
Create a simple layout on the VM SSD:

D:\CyberLab\
  ISO\
  VMs\
  Exports\
  Evidence\
  Backups\

Keep original ISO files and checksums in ISO. Store exported sanitised evidence separately from VM disks. Do not treat snapshots as backups; copy important VM exports or data to a separate device.

docs.title: 4. First VM smoke test
docs.text:
Create an Ubuntu Server x86-64 VM: - Generation 2 / UEFI on Hyper-V. - 2 vCPU. - 4 GB RAM (dynamic memory may be enabled for this small utility VM). - 40 GB virtual disk. - NIC attached to the management-only/internal network during initial setup. - Attach the official Ubuntu Server x86-64 ISO.

Install using the Ubuntu installer. Create a non-root user, enable OpenSSH only if required, and apply updates. Record the Ubuntu release and kernel.

After boot:

uname -m
lsblk
ip -br address
ip route
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y

Expected architecture on this host: x86_64. If uname -m shows something else, stop and verify which ISO you installed.

docs.title: 5. Snapshots and baseline
docs.text:
Before installing agents or security tools: 1. Shut down the VM cleanly. 2. Create a snapshot/checkpoint named baseline-clean. 3. Record VM settings and guest OS version. 4. Boot and confirm the snapshot is visible. 5. Restore the snapshot once to prove the recovery workflow works.

For domain controllers and SIEM servers, use application-aware backups for persistent data; snapshots alone are not a safe backup strategy.

docs.title: 6. Validation checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Host CPU architecture is x64.
  • [ ] Firmware virtualisation is enabled.
  • [ ] Hypervisor starts after reboot.
  • [ ] Management and private networks are created.
  • [ ] No vulnerable/attacker VM is connected to a bridged network.
  • [ ] Ubuntu guest boots and reports x86_64.
  • [ ] VM storage is on SSD with sufficient free space.
  • [ ] Baseline snapshot/checkpoint can be restored.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Microsoft Hyper-V hardware requirements
  • Microsoft Hyper-V virtual switch documentation
  • VMware Workstation and Fusion FAQ

docs.title: Hardware and platform compatibility
docs.text: Planning guide — verify exact host models and versions

docs.title: 1. Confirm hardware before downloading images
docs.text:
On Windows PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object CsName, WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsArchitecture, CsTotalPhysicalMemory
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors, VirtualizationFirmwareEnabled, SecondLevelAddressTranslationExtensions
Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystemLabel, Size, SizeRemaining
systeminfo.exe

On Mac Terminal:

uname -m
system_profiler SPHardwareDataType
df -h /
sysctl hw.memsize

Expected Apple-silicon architecture: arm64. Record exact chip, RAM, macOS version and free storage.

For Hyper-V, confirm supported Windows edition, CPU SLAT, firmware virtualisation and DEP. Hyper-V is not available as a client feature on every Windows edition; if Windows Home is installed, use a supported alternative such as VMware Workstation.

docs.title: 2. Architecture compatibility matrix
docs.text:
Workload Windows x64 PC Apple-silicon Mac Windows 11 x64 guest Yes, with supported hypervisor No native x64 guest in Fusion; use Windows 11 ARM Windows 11 ARM guest Not on x64 Hyper-V host Yes, using supported ARM virtualisation Ubuntu x86-64 guest Yes No native x64 guest in Fusion Ubuntu ARM64 guest Depends on host hypervisor Yes Kali x86-64 guest Yes No native x64 guest in Fusion Kali ARM64 guest Depends on host hypervisor Yes Splunk Enterprise Supported x64 Windows/Linux platform ARM64 is not supported for Splunk Enterprise Splunk Universal Forwarder Supported platforms in current Splunk matrix Do not assume ARM64 support; check the exact Darwin architecture table Elastic Stack Supported x64 Linux deployment ARM64 Linux components are supported where listed in Elastic's current support matrix Wazuh central components Supported x64 Linux Supported 64-bit ARM Linux on listed OS versions Security Onion Yes, x86-64 only No; ARM is explicitly unsupported Zeek / Suricata Supported Linux builds ARM builds where the selected release/package supports them OWASP Juice Shop Docker image/platform must match guest Verify the published ARM64 image manifest

Apple Silicon limitation: VMware Fusion on Apple Silicon supports 64-bit ARM guests only; x86 guest operating systems are not supported. Windows 11 ARM guests have additional Fusion limitations: VBS, WSL2, Windows Sandbox and Windows Defender Application Guard require nested virtualisation and are not available in this configuration.

docs.title: 3. Practical planning allocations
docs.text:
These are home-lab planning recommendations, not vendor minimums for every component.

  • Windows PC: 32 GB RAM supports a reduced lab; 64 GB is a more useful target. Prefer 1 TB NVMe SSD or more and keep at least 150–250 GB free for VM disks and snapshots.
  • MacBook: 16 GB can run one small ARM Linux VM; 24 GB or more is preferable. Keep 150 GB free for a useful subset.
  • Security Onion Standalone: vendor bare minimum is 4 CPU cores, 24 GB RAM, 200 GB storage and 2 NICs. 32 GB RAM or more is a better home-lab target. It is x86-64 only.
  • Wazuh all-in-one quickstart: current official sizing for 1–25 agents is 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM and 50 GB storage for 90 days of indexed alert data. More agents/retention require more.
  • Elastic single-node lab: 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM and 150–200 GB is a practical starting point, not an Elastic production minimum.
  • Splunk: check current release-specific OS and hardware requirements. Do not treat generic RAM figures as official sizing.

Run one major SIEM stack at a time. Reserve memory for the host OS and hypervisor.

docs.title: 4. Media, support and licence checks
docs.text:
• Windows Server/Windows client media: Microsoft Evaluation Center/download pages; read the exact evaluation and activation terms.
  • Kali: official Kali images only; verify SHA-256.
  • VMware Fusion/Workstation: Broadcom's official portal; verify host and guest compatibility for exact release.
  • Splunk Enterprise and Universal Forwarder: current Splunk support matrix lists supported OS/architecture combinations. Splunk Enterprise does not support ARM architecture; Windows ARM is not a supported Enterprise/Universal Forwarder platform in the cited current matrix. Use x64 Windows/Linux on the PC.
  • Elastic: verify the exact Elasticsearch, Kibana, Agent and integration versions in Elastic's support matrix. Keep components on a compatible release family.
  • Wazuh: central components support x86_64/AMD64 and AARCH64/ARM64 Linux on listed OS versions.
  • Security Onion: x86-64 only.

docs.title: Lab 10 — Security Onion standalone monitoring (x86-64 only)
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

Security Onion is a separate network security monitoring platform. It is not an add-on to the Elastic/Wazuh VM. Use a dedicated x86-64 host/VM on the Windows PC and consult the current Security Onion 3 hardware and installation documentation before allocating resources. It does not support Apple-silicon ARM as a native deployment target.

docs.title: 1. Resource and topology
docs.text:
For a small standalone learning deployment, start with the vendor's current minimums as the floor, not a production sizing target. Security Onion can require substantial RAM, CPU, disk I/O and storage. Allocate a dedicated VM or spare x86-64 PC; do not run it alongside other full SIEM stacks on a 64 GB host.

Recommended logical interfaces: - Management interface: MGMT network, static address and gateway as required. - Monitoring interface: SENSOR network, receives mirrored traffic, no IP/gateway and no management access. - Optional storage: dedicated SSD-backed virtual disk with sufficient capacity.

The monitoring interface must receive traffic. A NIC attached to an empty private switch sees no network traffic.

docs.title: 2. Prepare installer
docs.text:
1. Download the current Security Onion ISO from its official download page.
  2. Verify the published checksum.
  3. Confirm the target is x86-64 and meets the current hardware requirements.
  4. Create a dedicated VM with the supported firmware/virtualisation configuration and enough disk.
  5. Attach the ISO and boot.
  6. Follow the current installation wizard and choose the Standalone deployment type only for a single-node lab.
  7. Configure management networking as requested by the installer.
  8. Complete setup and save credentials securely.

Installer prompts and supported deployment modes can change between releases. Use the current official installation guide, not screenshots from older versions.

docs.title: 3. Configure packet visibility
docs.text:
Before expecting alerts: 1. Configure the hypervisor or lab firewall to mirror selected endpoint/DMZ traffic to the sensor capture NIC. 2. Confirm the monitoring NIC is assigned as the sniffing interface in Security Onion. 3. Confirm the interface is not used for management, has no default route and does not forward packets. 4. Generate a known benign connection between two lab VMs. 5. Confirm packets are visible using the Security Onion interface and supported capture tooling.

Do not enable promiscuous mode and assume that this creates a mirror. Hypervisor port mirroring or an explicit network tap/bridge is required for traffic not addressed to the sensor.

docs.title: 4. Validate ingestion and detections
docs.text:
1. Confirm sensor services and health in the Security Onion interface.
  2. Generate benign DNS and HTTP traffic between lab endpoints and the Juice Shop target.
  3. Confirm the expected network metadata appears.
  4. Inspect the timestamp, source/destination, protocol and sensor interface.
  5. If an alert is generated, review the rule/signature and raw event before interpreting it.
  6. Document packet loss, capture gaps, rule version and retention.

Security Onion's component set and data schemas are release-dependent. Use the current vendor docs for SOC UI, Hunt, Alerts, Cases, Elastic Agent and sensor health procedures.

docs.title: 5. Safe operation
docs.text:
• Never attach the monitoring interface to a bridged home network.
  • Never expose the Security Onion management UI to the Internet.
  • Use only synthetic traffic generated in the lab.
  • Plan disk capacity and retention before storing PCAP.
  • Treat packet captures as sensitive; they may contain credentials or personal content.
  • Keep Security Onion isolated from other SIEM labs until the network and storage requirements are understood.

docs.title: Lab 11 — SOC validation exercises and operational monitoring
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This programme validates the full collection-to-investigation chain. Run each exercise in the SIEM currently powered on. Do not attempt to deploy every platform at once.

docs.title: 1. Define monitoring coverage
docs.text:
Create an asset inventory for the lab:

Asset Role Telemetry source Owner Expected heartbeat PSV-DC01 AD DS/DNS Windows Security, DNS Lab admin Agent/forwarder health PSV-W11-01 Windows endpoint Sysmon, Security, PowerShell Lab admin Agent/forwarder health Ubuntu endpoint Linux endpoint auditd, system logs, system metrics Lab admin Agent health Kali Assessment source System/auth logs; test record Lab admin Optional SIEM host Log platform Platform/service health Lab admin Service health Sensor Network monitoring Zeek/Suricata/PCAP metadata Lab admin Sensor health

For every source document event generation, collection, parsing, storage, searchability, alerting and retention. A green agent status does not prove all required event channels are collected.

docs.title: 2. Exercise A — Windows process creation
docs.text:
1. Confirm Sysmon Event ID 1 is generated locally.
  2. Confirm the same event reaches Elastic or Splunk.
  3. Compare host, image, command line, parent and process GUID fields.
  4. Run the Phase 5 encoded PowerShell analytic's positive and negative tests on the disposable endpoint.
  5. Confirm positive matches and negative no-match.
  6. Record the raw event, query, rule version, alert, timestamps and collection delay.

Use only a harmless test command in your own VM. Do not execute downloaded payloads or real malware.

docs.title: 3. Exercise B — local Administrators group change
docs.text:
On a disposable Windows endpoint, create a synthetic local test user and add it to the local Administrators group only for the controlled exercise. Record the exact before/after membership and use an approved local admin session.

Verify the Windows Security log contains Event ID 4732 and the target group SID is S-1-5-32-544. Forward the event to the SIEM. Run the Phase 5 detection and confirm: - Positive: target SID is the built-in Administrators SID. - Negative: an event for another group (for example Users) does not match. - Actor, member, target SID, host and time are parsed correctly.

Remove the test user from the group and delete the synthetic account. Confirm the cleanup event is also recorded. Do not run this on a production or personal daily-use machine.

docs.title: 4. Exercise C — Linux authentication and audit
docs.text:
1. Confirm auditd is installed and active on Ubuntu.
  2. Generate a successful login to the test account and a failed login using a deliberately incorrect password.
  3. Confirm source records exist in the journal/auth log and audit log where configured.
  4. Forward the records to the selected SIEM.
  5. Verify username, source, event time and result are parsed correctly.
  6. Record whether the SIEM distinguishes failed authentication from successful login.

Do not brute-force accounts. A single controlled failed login is sufficient to validate collection.

docs.title: 5. Exercise D — network monitoring
docs.text:
1. Generate a DNS query from a lab endpoint to the lab DNS server.
  2. Generate HTTP traffic to the Juice Shop target.
  3. Confirm the sensor sees the traffic on the intended capture interface.
  4. Confirm Zeek logs the expected connection/DNS metadata.
  5. Confirm Suricata processes the packet and writes EVE output.
  6. Correlate endpoint, DNS and sensor records using IP, time and other available identifiers.

If sensor packets are missing, check SPAN/mirroring, VLAN, NIC mapping, asymmetric routing, capture drops and time synchronisation before changing rules.

docs.title: 6. Exercise E — health and availability monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor: - Agent/forwarder last-seen and policy state. - SIEM node health, cluster status and disk watermarks. - Indexing/ingest errors and queue/backpressure. - CPU, RAM, swap, disk I/O latency and free storage. - Sensor interface status, packet drops and capture throughput. - Clock synchronisation and event ingestion delay. - Backup/restore and snapshot status.

Set thresholds based on measured baseline and vendor guidance. Avoid arbitrary universal thresholds. Alert on loss of telemetry as well as security events.

docs.title: 7. Exercise F — investigation and case management
docs.text:
For one synthetic alert: 1. Create a case with unique lab case ID. 2. Preserve the raw source event and SIEM alert. 3. Build a UTC timeline retaining original timezone. 4. Correlate host, user, process GUID, session, IP and transaction-like test reference where relevant. 5. Record confirmed facts separately from hypotheses. 6. Document false-positive assessment, evidence gaps and decision. 7. Add remediation and retest evidence. 8. Close the case with reviewer and date.

Use the Phase 5 fraud/incident templates as structures, not as proof of regulatory compliance.

docs.title: 8. Evidence package
docs.text:
For each exercise save: - Hardware and hypervisor details. - VM settings and IP/network diagram. - Exact OS and product versions. - Relevant configuration (sanitised). - Original local event and SIEM copy. - Search/query and rule versions. - Expected vs actual result. - Timestamps and ingest latency. - Troubleshooting and cleanup. - Limitations and reviewer sign-off.

Use synthetic accounts and addresses. Do not upload production telemetry, customer records, internal hostnames or credentials to PSV.

docs.title: 9. Exit criteria
docs.text: A lab is complete only when: - Network isolation is proven. - Source event generation is verified locally. - SIEM ingestion and parsing are verified. - Positive and negative tests pass. - Alert context supports analyst triage. - Telemetry-health gaps are documented. - Cleanup is verified. - The evidence package is reproducible by another person.

  • Elastic detection rule concepts

docs.title: Lab 6 — Splunk Enterprise and Universal Forwarder
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

This is a separate Splunk deployment. Use a supported x86-64 Windows or Linux server on the Windows PC. The Mac is an endpoint/admin client; do not assume Splunk Enterprise server is supported natively on Apple-silicon macOS.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
Windows endpoint (Sysmon + Universal Forwarder) → TCP receiving port → Splunk Enterprise → Search & Reporting.

Use a dedicated VM. Do not run Splunk, Elastic, Wazuh and Security Onion together on a resource-constrained host.

docs.title: 2. Install Splunk Enterprise
docs.text:
1. Download the current Splunk Enterprise installer from Splunk's official download portal.
  2. Check current supported OS, architecture, RAM, disk and licence terms.
  3. Select a supported x86-64 platform from the current support matrix.
  4. For Linux, follow Splunk's release-specific package installation instructions. A Debian package workflow is shown below; replace placeholders with the exact downloaded filename:
sudo dpkg -i splunk-<version>-<build>-linux-amd64.deb
sudo /opt/splunk/bin/splunk start --accept-license
sudo /opt/splunk/bin/splunk enable boot-start
  1. For Windows, run the signed MSI as Administrator and follow the installer. Record the actual install path.
  2. Set a strong unique admin password and store it securely.
  3. Confirm the service is running and open Splunk Web from MGMT only.

docs.title: 3. Enable receiving
docs.text:
In Splunk Web, go to Settings → Forwarding and receiving → Configure receiving → New Receiving Port. Configure TCP 9997 (or another explicitly selected port). Restrict inbound access to the endpoint subnet.

Verify on Linux:

sudo ss -lntp | grep 9997

On Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 9997 -State Listen

Do not expose management port 8089 or Web port 8000 to untrusted networks.

docs.title: 4. Create a test index
docs.text: Create an index named windows_lab under Settings → Indexes. Record its retention and storage policy. Use a disposable lab index, not production.

docs.title: 5. Install Universal Forwarder on Windows endpoint
docs.text:
1. Download the current Windows x64 Universal Forwarder MSI from Splunk.
  2. Confirm compatibility with the Enterprise version.
  3. Install on PSV-W11-01.
  4. Configure the receiving Splunk host and port using the installer wizard or current Splunk CLI.
  5. Configure the Sysmon Operational channel input. A starting stanza is:
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
index = windows_lab
renderXml = 1

Confirm the channel name and stanza syntax against the current Universal Forwarder documentation. Do not assume the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows or CIM field extractions are present.

  1. Configure outputs.conf with the actual server address and port:
[tcpout]
defaultGroup = lab-indexer

[tcpout:lab-indexer]
server = 10.10.30.21:9997
  1. Restart the forwarder using the supported service/CLI method and inspect its internal logs.

docs.title: 6. Verify ingestion
docs.text:
Search:

index=windows_lab earliest=-15m
| stats count by host sourcetype source

Then inspect Sysmon process events:

index=windows_lab EventCode=1
| table _time host Image CommandLine ParentImage ProcessGuid
| sort -_time

Field names vary with raw XML, add-ons and parsing. If EventCode or Image is absent, inspect raw events and adapt the query. A running forwarder service is not proof of ingestion.

docs.title: 7. Test the Phase 5 detection
docs.text: Use the PowerShell encoded-command detection only after confirming the real field names. Run positive and negative test cases on the disposable endpoint. Record raw event, search result, field extraction and any benign positives. Do not use production indexes.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Confirm the local Sysmon event exists.
  • Check forwarder service status and internal logs.
  • Confirm outputs.conf destination, port, DNS and firewall.
  • Confirm Splunk receiving is enabled and the test index exists.
  • Check index permissions and time range.
  • Inspect raw XML before changing field names.
  • Avoid duplicate collection of the same channel by multiple agents.

docs.title: 9. Licence note
docs.text: Splunk licence and trial/free capabilities change. Check current terms from Splunk before downloading; do not assume an evaluation remains fully functional after expiry.

docs.text:

docs.title: Lab 7 — Wazuh all-in-one SOC stack
docs.text:
Build guide — not yet lab-tested

The all-in-one Wazuh deployment places manager, indexer and dashboard on one Linux host for learning. It is not a highly available production architecture.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the server
docs.text:
Use a fresh supported Ubuntu Server VM on the Windows PC or Mac. Wazuh central components support 64-bit Intel, AMD and ARM Linux on the operating systems listed in the current support matrix. For a 1–25 agent quickstart, Wazuh currently recommends 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM and 50 GB storage for 90 days of indexed alert data; use more disk for raw logs and longer retention. Run Wazuh separately from Elastic and Splunk initially.

Set hostname and static address, update the OS, and confirm DNS/time are correct. Do not expose the dashboard to the public Internet.

docs.title: 2. Install using the official assistant
docs.text:
1. Open the current Wazuh Quickstart documentation and confirm the current version, OS support and sizing. At the time this guide was checked, the official page documents Wazuh 4.14 and the following assistant command. If the current docs show a newer version, use that documented version instead:
curl -sO https://packages.wazuh.com/4.14/wazuh-install.sh
sudo bash ./wazuh-install.sh -a
  1. Run the assistant on the fresh server.
  2. Save the generated dashboard credentials and certificates securely.
  3. Confirm services:
sudo systemctl status wazuh-manager --no-pager
sudo systemctl status wazuh-indexer --no-pager
sudo systemctl status wazuh-dashboard --no-pager
  1. Access the dashboard over the management network using HTTPS and the generated trust material. Do not permanently disable certificate validation.

docs.title: 3. Enrol Windows endpoint
docs.text:
1. In the dashboard, open Agents → Deploy new agent.
  2. Select Windows and the current agent package.
  3. Enter the Wazuh manager address reachable on SERVER.
  4. Copy the generated installation/enrolment command.
  5. Run it in elevated PowerShell on PSV-W11-01.
  6. Start the Wazuh service and confirm the agent appears active.

Generated commands may contain registration secrets and internal addresses. Never publish them.

docs.title: 4. Enrol Linux endpoint
docs.text:
1. Open Deploy new agent and select the correct Linux distribution and architecture.
  2. Follow the current repository and package instructions.
  3. Configure the manager address and enrol the agent.
  4. Enable/start the agent and verify it appears active.

docs.title: 5. Validate telemetry
docs.text:
• Check agent status and last keepalive.
  • Inspect manager and agent logs for connection or decoder errors.
  • Generate a harmless test event, such as creating/modifying a file in a dedicated FIM test directory.
  • Confirm the event is visible in the dashboard.
  • Record agent ID, rule ID, decoder, source log, event time and raw event.

Installing an agent does not automatically enable every capability. File Integrity Monitoring, vulnerability detection, Security Configuration Assessment, command auditing and log collection have separate configuration and coverage requirements.

docs.title: 6. First exercises
docs.text:
1. Configure FIM for a dedicated lab directory using the current Wazuh FIM documentation.
  2. Create, modify and delete a harmless test file.
  3. Verify the expected alert and identify the rule that generated it.
  4. Configure collection of the Sysmon Operational channel on Windows.
  5. Generate a benign Notepad process event.
  6. Compare the Wazuh event with the original Event Viewer record.

Use a version-controlled copy of custom rules. Validate configuration before restarting services. Do not paste unreviewed example rules into a production manager.

docs.title: 7. Troubleshooting and cleanup
docs.text: Check manager/indexer/dashboard service logs, agent connectivity, DNS, firewall, certificates, disk and memory. Unenrol agents through the supported workflow. Do not delete indexer data directories manually while services are running.

docs.title: Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic
docs.text:
Reference design — not yet lab-tested

This walkthrough describes a safe, reproducible design for collecting Windows process-creation telemetry and reviewing it in Elastic. It is a build plan, not evidence that this environment has been deployed or tested. Record the exact Windows, Sysmon, Elastic Agent, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions before marking it tested.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Generate one benign process event on an isolated Windows virtual machine, confirm that Sysmon records it, collect the event with Elastic, and verify that the event can be searched and interpreted.

Success criteria

  1. A controlled process launch produces a Sysmon Process Create event (Event ID 1).
  2. The event is visible in the local Sysmon Operational log.
  3. The configured collection agent forwards the event to the expected Elastic data stream.
  4. The event contains enough context to identify the process and its parent.
  5. The write-up records any missing fields, collection delay, and configuration limitations.

docs.title: Scope and safety
docs.text:
• Use a Windows VM that you own or are explicitly authorised to administer.
  • Use Notepad as the benign test process. Do not use malware, exploit code, credential dumping, persistence payloads, or live suspicious indicators.
  • Prefer a host-only or otherwise restricted virtual network. Permit only the management and telemetry connectivity required by your lab.
  • Do not connect this exercise to production endpoints or production SIEM data.
  • Do not paste real user, customer, or employer telemetry into public tools.

docs.title: Reference architecture
docs.text:
Windows test VM
  └─ Sysmon service
       └─ Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational
            └─ Elastic Agent (Windows integration)
                 └─ Elasticsearch
                      └─ Kibana Discover

The Elastic Windows integration documents collection of Windows-specific channels including Sysmon and PowerShell. The Sysmon data stream is named windows.sysmon_operational in the integration documentation. Confirm the actual data stream and field mappings in your own version before using saved queries.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A supported Windows 10 or Windows 11 VM with administrative access. On Windows 11, check whether the built-in Sysmon optional feature is available in your edition/build.
  • Sysmon downloaded from Microsoft's official Sysinternals page.
  • An Elastic environment with a compatible Elastic Agent and Windows integration, or an equivalent approved log collector.
  • Sufficient disk space for the VM and a snapshot taken before configuration.
  • A written record of versions, VM network mode, host name, and collection configuration.

Official references:

  • Microsoft: Enable and configure Sysmon in Windows
  • Microsoft Sysmon download and usage
  • Microsoft Sysmon event reference
  • Elastic Windows integration

docs.title: 1. Prepare the endpoint
docs.text:
1. Create or select an isolated Windows VM.
  2. Apply the updates required for the lab and record the OS build.
  3. Take a VM snapshot.
  4. Confirm the VM can reach only the required management and telemetry endpoints.
  5. Record the local time zone. Sysmon event timestamps are recorded in UTC.

docs.title: 2. Install and verify Sysmon
docs.text:
Windows 11 now offers Sysmon as a built-in optional feature, while the standalone Sysinternals download remains available. Choose one installation method appropriate to the VM and Windows version; do not install the built-in feature and standalone package on top of one another.

  1. Check whether Sysmon is already installed before making changes:
Get-Service sysmon*
  1. For Windows 11, review Microsoft's current instructions for enabling the built-in optional feature. For Windows 10, or where you deliberately choose the standalone package, download Sysmon from the official Microsoft Sysinternals page. Verify the download source and publisher.
  2. Review the current Microsoft usage instructions before installation; command-line options can change between Sysmon releases.
  3. Install or enable Sysmon with an approved configuration. For this first exercise, ensure Process Create telemetry is enabled.
  4. Open Event Viewer and navigate to Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational.
  5. Confirm the channel is present, Sysmon is running, and new events are being written.

Sysmon Event ID 1 records process creation, including process and parent-process context. Network connection events (Event ID 3) are disabled by default, so do not expect them unless you deliberately enable them in the configuration.

docs.title: 3. Generate a benign event
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in the test VM and run:

Start-Process -FilePath "$env:WINDIR\System32\notepad.exe" -PassThru |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName

Close Notepad normally after confirming it started.

In Event Viewer, inspect the newest Sysmon Process Create event. Confirm that the image, process ID, command line, parent process, user, and timestamp fields are populated where available. The exact values depend on the VM and Sysmon configuration.

You can also inspect recent events with PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
    Id      = 1
} -MaxEvents 10 |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message

docs.title: 4. Configure collection
docs.text:
In Elastic Fleet, enrol an Elastic Agent on the Windows VM and add the Windows integration according to the official integration guide. Enable the Sysmon Operational channel/data stream.

Do not assume that adding the integration proves collection is working. Check agent health, integration policy, permissions, data stream creation, and the arrival of a new event generated after the policy was applied.

If you use a different SIEM or collector, document the equivalent source channel, collection method, destination, parsing stage, and field mapping.

docs.title: 5. Search and verify
docs.text:
In Kibana Discover, select the relevant Sysmon data view and search for the test process. A starting KQL example is:

event.dataset : "windows.sysmon_operational"
and event.code : "1"
and process.name : "notepad.exe"

The integration's field mappings and dataset names can vary by version and configuration. If the query returns no results, inspect the raw event and the data view before changing the query. Do not interpret a failed query as proof that no event was generated.

For the matching event, record:

  • @timestamp and the source event time
  • event.dataset and event.code
  • host.name
  • process.name, process.executable, and process.command_line
  • process.pid and process.entity_id, if present
  • process.parent.name, process.parent.executable, and parent process ID, if present
  • user.name, if present
  • The time at which the event became searchable

docs.title: 6. Validate the collection path
docs.text:
Check Expected evidence If it fails Sysmon installed Sysmon service and Operational channel exist Review installation and service status Event generated Event ID 1 for the Notepad process Check Sysmon configuration and event time Agent healthy Agent is enrolled and policy is applied Review agent status, permissions, and connectivity Data received New Sysmon document appears in the expected data stream Check integration channel, agent logs, and ingest errors Fields usable Process and host fields are searchable Inspect the raw event and parsing/mapping Timeline consistent Source time precedes or matches ingestion time Check time zones, clock synchronisation, and pipeline delay

A local event with no corresponding SIEM document indicates a collection or ingestion problem, not a detection failure. A document with missing fields indicates a parsing, mapping, or source-configuration issue that should be diagnosed separately.

docs.title: Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• Verify the Sysmon service is running and the Operational channel is enabled.
  • Confirm Event ID 1 is not excluded by the Sysmon configuration.
  • Generate a new event after the collector policy is active; do not rely only on older events.
  • Confirm the Elastic Agent policy includes the Windows integration and Sysmon channel.
  • Check agent health, network reachability, permissions, ingest pipeline errors, and data-stream naming.
  • Compare the raw event with the parsed document before changing field names in a query.
  • Check endpoint and SIEM clock synchronisation and compare source event time with ingestion time.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
1. Close the test process.
  2. If Sysmon was installed only for this exercise, remove it using the uninstall procedure documented by Microsoft.
  3. Remove or unenrol the test agent only if it is no longer required.
  4. Retain or delete lab data according to your lab retention policy.
  5. Revert the VM snapshot if you want to return to the original state.

docs.title: Evidence record
docs.text:
Before changing the status to Lab-tested, attach or record:

  • Windows edition/build and VM platform
  • Sysmon version and configuration hash or version
  • Elastic Agent, integration, Elasticsearch, and Kibana versions
  • Sanitised screenshot or export of the local Event ID 1
  • Sanitised SIEM document showing the same process event
  • Query used and exact fields observed
  • Collection delay and any troubleshooting performed
  • Cleanup result and date last verified

Current status: Reference design only. No execution results are claimed by this page.

docs.text:

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
A structured learning map for infrastructure, monitoring, detection engineering, application security, investigations, and reliable security operations.

The curriculum uses recognised standards and primary technical specifications where they apply. The Industry Standards & Authoritative References page records the publisher, version, scope, and limitations of each source.

D01Infrastructure & Platform FoundationNetworking, operating systems, virtualisation, cloud, telemetry foundations, and platform operations. D02Security Monitoring & DetectionTelemetry engineering, SIEM data quality, Sigma, ATT&CK, detection testing, and alert operations. D03Offensive Security & TestingAuthorised testing, OWASP ASVS verification, vulnerability validation, CVSS, and reporting. D04Security Operations & InvestigationsNIST incident response, evidence provenance, account takeover investigation, and SAMA counter-fraud references. D05Operations, Maintenance & CapstoneChange, service health, vulnerability management, recovery, automation, and operational evidence.

docs.title: How to use the learning paths
docs.text:
1. Start with the relevant domain and authoritative source.
  2. Check the version, scope, and applicability before using a requirement.
  3. Separate the source requirement from the implementation example.
  4. Work through the practical exercise in an authorised environment.
  5. Record versions, commands, expected results, raw evidence, and observed results.
  6. Link the exercise to a lab or investigation where relevant.
  7. Record limitations and the date the material was last reviewed.

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text:
• Standard / framework reference: a direct reference to a published source.
  • Implementation guidance: a practical interpretation, not a verbatim requirement.
  • Lab-tested: executed in a controlled environment with evidence recorded.
  • Simulated scenario: synthetic material for learning.
  • Research note: reviewed against documentation but not independently executed.

Unfinished work will not be presented as complete. A control mapping is not proof of compliance, and a sample exercise is not a formal assessment.

docs.title: D01 — Infrastructure & Platform Foundation
docs.text: Understand the systems and network services on which applications and security controls depend.

docs.title: Build the lab foundation
docs.text: Follow the PSV enterprise-style home lab programme, beginning with hardware compatibility, hypervisor installation and network segmentation. The Windows PC and Apple-silicon Mac have separate build instructions.

docs.title: Learning areas
docs.text:
• Networking: Ethernet, IPv4/IPv6, subnetting, routing, switching, VLANs, TCP/UDP, DNS, DHCP, HTTP/S, and TLS.
  • Linux: users and permissions, processes, services, storage, filesystems, logs, SSH, and systemd.
  • Windows: accounts, services, Event Viewer, PowerShell, process creation, and basic domain concepts.
  • Virtualisation and containers: hypervisors, virtual networks, images, containers, and resource allocation.
  • Platform operations: storage, CPU and memory, backups, patching, and availability.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text: Build a small isolated network with one Linux system and one Windows system. Document the addressing plan, DNS resolution, connectivity tests, user permissions, service status, and relevant system logs.

docs.title: Evidence to record
docs.text:
Environment and software versions; network diagram and private lab IP plan; commands and expected results; troubleshooting and root cause; security implications and references.

D02 uses this foundation to understand telemetry. D04 uses it to correlate endpoint, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: Authoritative references
docs.text:
• NIST CSF 2.0 — cybersecurity outcomes and risk-management context.
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — prioritised safeguards for implementation planning.

docs.title: Protocol and addressing references
docs.text:
Use primary protocol specifications when documenting network behaviour. Examples include:

  • RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 — DNS concepts and implementation.
  • RFC 1918 — IPv4 private address allocation.
  • RFC 5737 — IPv4 documentation address blocks; these are for examples and documentation, not real public endpoints.
  • RFC 4291 — IPv6 addressing architecture.
  • RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3 protocol.
  • RFC 9110 — HTTP semantics.

An RFC is a publication series, not a guarantee that every RFC is an Internet Standard. Check each document's status and updates on the RFC Editor site before treating it as a normative requirement.

docs.title: D02 — Security Monitoring & Detection
docs.text: Learn how security telemetry is collected, normalised, searched, correlated, and converted into detections that can be tested and maintained.

docs.title: Hands-on SIEM labs
docs.text: Build and validate Elastic, Splunk or Wazuh one at a time. Add Zeek/Suricata or Security Onion only after packet visibility and resource requirements are confirmed.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST CSF 2.0 — use the Detect Function outcomes to structure monitoring and adverse-event analysis.
  • MITRE ATT&CK — describe adversary behaviour using supported tactic and technique references; do not infer attribution from a technique match.
  • Sigma Specification 2.1.0 — author portable detection logic using the published rule structure and condition semantics.
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — use applicable safeguards to inform monitoring and operational priorities.

docs.title: 1. Telemetry engineering
docs.text:
A detection is only as reliable as its data source and field semantics. For each source, document:

  • System, product, version, host role, and collection method
  • Event channel, event ID or dataset, and audit policy/configuration
  • Required fields and their source-native meaning
  • Timestamp source, time zone, clock synchronisation, and ingestion delay
  • Parsing, normalisation, enrichment, and field-mapping stages
  • Retention, access control, integrity protection, and data owner
  • Known blind spots and conditions that stop events being generated

Do not assume that identically named fields mean the same thing across Windows Event Log, Sysmon, Elastic ECS, Splunk CIM, or a vendor-specific schema. Validate field mappings against raw records from the deployed version.

docs.title: 2. Detection engineering lifecycle
docs.text:
Use the following lifecycle for every detection change. This is an operational workflow informed by NIST CSF and Sigma; it is not a verbatim sequence mandated by either source.

  1. Define the analytic question. State the behaviour or security outcome being monitored.
  2. Identify required telemetry. Record source, event types, audit settings, fields, and collection dependencies.
  3. Describe the behaviour. Map to MITRE ATT&CK only where the behaviour and evidence support the technique.
  4. Author the analytic. Use the target SIEM's native language or a Sigma rule with a defined logsource and condition.
  5. Validate syntax and semantics. Parse against the relevant schema; for Sigma, use a maintained Sigma toolchain and confirm backend support.
  6. Test against evidence. Use known-positive, known-negative, and benign administrative samples. Record the test dataset and expected result.
  7. Measure operational impact. Review event volume, false positives, duplicates, latency, query cost, and analyst context.
  8. Approve and deploy. Use the organisation's change process, version control, peer review, and rollback plan.
  9. Monitor and maintain. Review performance, data-source health, rule status, environment changes, and threat changes.

A rule that parses is not necessarily correct. A query that returns events is not necessarily a useful detection. A clean test set does not establish production effectiveness.

docs.title: 3. Sigma rule structure
docs.text:
The Sigma Rules Specification 2.1.0 defines required and optional fields including title, logsource, detection, and condition. It also defines search identifiers, logical conditions, value modifiers, status, tags, and schema.

A minimal illustrative rule structure is shown below. This is a syntax example, not a validated production detection:

title: Example Process Creation Analytic
status: test
description: Illustrates the structure of a process-creation rule.
logsource:
    product: windows
    category: process_creation
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\example.exe'
    condition: selection
level: low

The sample uses an intentionally generic executable name and is not intended to detect malicious activity. The level value is Sigma metadata, not a universal incident priority or response SLA.

Official references: - Sigma Rules Specification - Sigma specification repository and JSON schemas - Sigma rule-writing guide

docs.title: 4. ATT&CK mapping discipline
docs.text:
For each mapped detection, record:

  • ATT&CK domain and release/data version used
  • Technique or sub-technique ID and name
  • The exact event behaviour that supports the mapping
  • Whether the analytic detects the technique directly, a related observable, or only a prerequisite
  • Data-source requirements and known coverage gaps
  • Test evidence and confidence

Do not claim full technique coverage because one analytic has an ATT&CK tag. ATT&CK is a knowledge base for describing behaviour; the quality of a detection depends on telemetry, logic, testing, and operational context.

docs.title: 5. Alert quality and operational acceptance
docs.text:
Before production use, define and measure the criteria approved by the organisation. Useful measures include:

  • Detection test pass/fail against a versioned test set
  • Alert volume by source and rule
  • Confirmed true-positive, benign-positive, and false-positive outcomes using the organisation's definitions
  • Time from event occurrence to searchable telemetry
  • Time from alert creation to analyst acknowledgement and disposition
  • Percentage of alerts with required investigation context
  • Data-source health and missing-event rates

Do not invent universal thresholds for these measures. Set targets from the service's risk, baseline, coverage, staffing, and approved service-level objectives.

docs.title: 6. Applied lab
docs.text: Continue with the Windows Endpoint Telemetry: Sysmon to Elastic lab. It is explicitly a reference design until the actual Windows build, Sysmon configuration, Elastic integration version, event, and search result are recorded.

docs.title: 7. Operational detection pack
docs.text:
The PSV Detection Engineering Pack contains two example detections with Sigma source, Elastic KQL and Splunk SPL starting queries, synthetic test cases, telemetry requirements, triage steps, and release gates:

  • PowerShell encoded-command execution (Sysmon Event ID 1)
  • Addition to the built-in local Administrators group (Windows Security Event ID 4732)

These are test-status examples. The backend queries are authored starting points based on stated field assumptions, not confirmed output from a specific live SIEM. CI validates both Sigma files against the Sigma 2.1.0 schema and converts them to Splunk SPL with the applicable Sysmon and Splunk Windows pipelines. This does not validate the queries against a live SIEM; test them against raw events from your own environment.

docs.title: Evidence record for a detection change
docs.text:
Record Required detail Change identity Rule ID, version, author, reviewer, date Purpose Behaviour and security question Data dependency Source, event IDs/dataset, audit configuration, fields Logic Sigma or native query and exact backend/version Validation Parser/schema result and test cases Results Positive/negative tests, observed output, false positives Operations Volume, latency, cost, owner, escalation path Change control Approval, deployment time, rollback Maintenance Review date, related threat/data changes

Operational note: Detection examples are not production-ready until adapted to the actual event schema and tested in the target environment.

docs.title: D03 — Offensive Security & Application Testing
docs.text: Use authorised testing to identify, validate, explain, and help remediate security weaknesses. This domain focuses on evidence-based verification rather than tool output alone.

docs.title: Isolated assessment environment
docs.text: Use the PSV penetration-testing lab with Kali and deliberately vulnerable targets on a dedicated, non-bridged network. Verify isolation before scanning.

docs.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 5.0.0
docs.text:
OWASP ASVS provides testable security requirements for web applications and web services. Use the requirement identifiers and verification guidance from the selected ASVS release. Record the exact version and requirement ID in test evidence.

ASVS is a verification standard. The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document about prominent application security risks; it is not a substitute for a complete verification plan.

Official sources: - OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 - OWASP ASVS project

docs.title: FIRST CVSS v4.0
docs.text:
CVSS v4.0 defines Base, Threat, Environmental, and Supplemental metric groups. A Base score communicates technical vulnerability severity under the CVSS model; it does not by itself determine organisational risk or remediation priority.

For each finding, preserve: - CVE or other vulnerability identifier, if one exists - Affected product and exact version/configuration - Reproduction conditions and evidence - CVSS version, score, and full vector - Threat and environmental assumptions - Asset criticality, exposure, compensating controls, and business context - Remediation recommendation and retest evidence

Official source: FIRST CVSS v4.0 specification.

PSV tool limitation: the current calculator on the Tools page implements CVSS v3.1, not v4.0. Do not enter a v4.0 vector into it or report its result as CVSS v4.0.

docs.title: Testing workflow
docs.text:
1. Authorisation and scope: written permission, in-scope assets, excluded systems, dates, source IPs, test accounts, and emergency contacts.
  2. Rules of engagement: allowed techniques, rate limits, data-handling requirements, stop conditions, and reporting route.
  3. Reconnaissance: use only approved sources and methods; record timestamps and evidence.
  4. Validation: confirm the weakness with the least intrusive method that proves the issue.
  5. Impact assessment: describe confidentiality, integrity, availability, affected roles, preconditions, and realistic boundaries.
  6. Reporting: include exact affected asset/version, reproducible steps, sanitised evidence, severity methodology, and practical remediation.
  7. Retesting: verify the fix using the same relevant conditions and record the result.

docs.title: Practical exercise
docs.text:
Use an intentionally vulnerable local application. Select an ASVS requirement that is relevant to the application's feature, define a safe test, record expected and observed behaviour, and explain whether the requirement is satisfied. Do not claim ASVS compliance from a small sample of tests.

Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Avoid destructive payloads, production data, persistence, or unnecessary service disruption.

docs.title: Finding record
docs.text:
Field What to capture Scope Asset, owner, environment, authorisation reference Requirement ASVS version and requirement ID, if applicable Weakness Accurate technical description and affected component Reproduction Preconditions, steps, and expected/observed result Evidence Sanitised request/response, logs, screenshots, timestamps Severity CVSS version, vector and score, plus contextual risk rationale Remediation Specific change and references Retest Build/version, test conditions, observed result, date

A scanner finding is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability. Validate applicability and exploitability before reporting it as confirmed.

docs.title: D04 — Security Operations & Investigations
docs.text: Develop an evidence-led approach to suspicious activity across endpoint, network, identity, application, transaction, and fraud-monitoring systems.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 — current NIST incident-response guidance, finalised April 2025; it supersedes Rev. 2.
  • NIST CSF 2.0 — relevant outcomes include Detect, Respond, and Recover.
  • SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework — Banking Sector framework, subject to SAMA applicability.
  • SAMA 2025 Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements — separate requirements for payment systems and payment services providers; verify entity scope.
  • EMVCo 3-D Secure — authoritative 3DS protocol specifications and version bulletins.
  • MITRE ATT&CK — a knowledge base for describing observed adversary behaviour, not a verdict or attribution engine.

docs.title: 1. Separate security incidents from fraud cases
docs.text:
Security incident response and counter-fraud investigation can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

A single event may require parallel workstreams: - Cybersecurity incident handling for compromised endpoints, accounts, infrastructure, malware, or unauthorised access. - Counter-fraud case handling for suspicious customer or employee activity, unauthorised transactions, social engineering, account takeover, or attempted loss. - Payment operations, customer support, legal, compliance, and other stakeholder involvement according to the organisation's approved process.

Record the case owner, incident owner, hand-offs, and decision authority. Do not assume that one team can perform every containment, payment, customer-contact, or regulatory action.

docs.title: 2. Triage and prioritisation
docs.text:
NIST CSF 2.0 identifies incident triage and validation, categorisation and prioritisation, escalation, and recovery initiation as incident-management outcomes. Apply the organisation's approved severity and escalation model.

At minimum, capture:

  • What was observed, by which system, and at what time
  • Affected customer, account, device, application, service, or asset identifiers in the authorised case system
  • Potential ongoing loss, service impact, customer impact, and scope
  • Whether the activity is ongoing, stopped, or not yet established
  • Available evidence and telemetry gaps
  • Immediate actions already taken and by whom
  • Required escalation, decision owner, and next review time

Do not infer severity solely from a keyword, transaction value, CVSS score, ATT&CK technique, or a single fraud signal. Use the approved organisational model and documented impact assessment.

docs.title: 3. Investigation evidence and provenance
docs.text:
Preserve original records and record how evidence was obtained. For every important artefact, capture:

  • Source system, source record identifier, and collection method
  • Original timestamp, time zone, and normalised UTC timestamp
  • Collection timestamp and any ingestion delay
  • Collector or analyst identity and access context
  • Original value and any transformation or enrichment
  • Hash or integrity mechanism where appropriate and supported
  • Retention, access restrictions, and chain-of-custody requirements
  • Known gaps, clock skew, parsing errors, and source limitations

Do not overwrite original evidence with enriched values. Keep enrichment and analyst interpretation as separate fields or records.

docs.title: 4. Account takeover and transaction investigation
docs.text:
The following is a collection and correlation checklist, not a claim that any single signal proves account takeover.

Evidence domain Investigative questions Identity and authentication Was there a password reset, MFA change, new authenticator, failed-login sequence, unusual authentication method, or recovery-channel change? Device and session Is the device identifier stable and trustworthy? Are device fingerprint, app version, session ID, IP, ASN, and user-agent consistent across the available records? Customer profile Were phone, email, address, beneficiary, limit, or profile details changed before the disputed activity? Transaction What were amount, currency, channel, beneficiary, payment rail, timestamp, status, and authorisation outcome? Step-up and 3-D Secure What authentication flow was used? Capture the available 3DS version, transaction identifiers, ECI, result/status, challenge outcome, and liability-shift indicators where applicable and available. Do not treat a 3DS result as proof that the legitimate customer initiated the transaction. Application/API Are request IDs, trace IDs, gateway logs, application logs, and backend outcomes available? Did the transaction pass through expected services? Network and endpoint Are source IP, DNS, TLS, endpoint, proxy, and EDR records available to corroborate the session? Fraud controls Which rules/models fired, what data was evaluated, what decision was returned, and were any controls bypassed, disabled, or overridden? Customer contact Was the customer contacted through an independently verified channel? Record the result according to approved procedures.

docs.title: Device identifiers are not identity proof
docs.text: A device ID, cookie, app-generated identifier, or fingerprint can be copied, replayed, reset, or appear differently across application versions and collection layers. Treat it as one signal. Correlate it with server-side session records, authentication events, device attestation signals where implemented, application telemetry, and transaction evidence.

docs.title: 3-D Secure is not a standalone fraud verdict
docs.text: 3-D Secure data should be interpreted using the relevant EMV 3-D Secure specification and the payment provider's documented field semantics. Record the actual message fields and result codes received. Do not invent an authentication outcome from a generic “3DS passed” label.

docs.title: 5. SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework: banking-sector operational references
docs.text:
The SAMA 2022 Banking Sector Counter-Fraud Framework has four domains: Governance, Prevent, Detect, and Respond. Its Rulebook includes 3.3 (policy and procedures), 4.1 (risk management), 5.1 (fraud detection standards), 5.2 (fraud detection systems), 6.2 (alert and case management), and 6.3 (fraud investigation). In particular, 5.2 addresses data quality, behavioural baselining, rules, risk scoring, feedback loops, calibration, and system metrics. The framework states a minimum maturity level of 3 for Member Organisations, while applicability is subject to SAMA's notification and discretion. Confirm the legal entity's status and applicable obligations with Compliance.

A separate SAMA Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements framework became effective on 13 April 2026 for Finance Sector — Payment Systems and Payment Services Providers. Its section 4.1 contains specific elevated-risk controls, including real-time detection, 24/7 operation of fraud detection systems, timely protective actions, and stronger authentication requirements. Do not transfer those control IDs to the 2022 Banking Sector framework or assume the PSP scope applies to every bank.

For card-not-present transactions, interpret actual EMV 3DS message fields and result codes using the applicable EMVCo version and bulletin set, plus the implementation documentation of the issuer/acquirer/provider. A generic 3DS success label is not proof of legitimate customer initiation.

Official sources: - SAMA 2022 Counter-Fraud Framework - SAMA 2025 Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements - SAMA 2025 elevated-risk controls, section 4.1 - EMVCo 3-D Secure

docs.title: 6. Containment and response decisions
docs.text:
Containment may include account protection, transaction blocking, session revocation, credential reset, device restrictions, endpoint isolation, or service-level controls. These actions can affect customers and business operations.

Before acting, confirm: - The authority and approval path for the action - The specific account, transaction, endpoint, or service in scope - The evidence supporting the action and the risk of delay - Customer impact, payment reversibility, and downstream dependencies - Whether evidence must be preserved first - How the action will be recorded, reviewed, and reversed if incorrect

Use approved playbooks and escalation paths. This page does not authorise operational actions or define an organisation's response SLA.

docs.title: 7. Investigation conclusion format
docs.text:
A defensible report separates:

  1. Observed facts: directly supported by original records.
  2. Correlated facts: independently sourced records linked by validated identifiers and time.
  3. Analysis: interpretation of the combined evidence.
  4. Alternative explanations: plausible benign or non-malicious causes.
  5. Assessment: supported conclusion and confidence with rationale.
  6. Impact: confirmed and potential customer, financial, operational, and security impact.
  7. Evidence gaps: unavailable logs, uncertain attribution, incomplete retention, or unverified data.
  8. Actions: decisions, approvals, owner, timestamp, and outcome.
  9. Follow-up: control improvement, monitoring, customer communication, recovery, and lessons learned.

Avoid absolute conclusions when the evidence is incomplete. “Not observed in available logs” is not the same as “did not occur.”

docs.title: Applied operational playbooks
docs.text:
• Account Takeover (ATO) Investigation Playbook — evidence preservation, cross-system correlation, missing-session log investigation, device-ID cloning/replay hypotheses, and decision records.
  • Payment Fraud Investigation Playbook — payment lifecycle, card/3DS evidence, SADAD-style payment flow, fraud-control evaluation, and reconciliation.
  • Fraud Investigation Case Record — blank case evidence template.

These are operational reference checklists, not substitutes for the institution's approved procedures, authority matrix, scheme rules, or regulatory advice.

docs.text:
